analysis.one_liner: Expands federal workplace safety law to government workers, strengthens whistleblower protections, and sharply raises penalties on unsafe employers.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 2025 with 41 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no hearing, markup, or floor vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 in several major ways. It would extend federal workplace safety coverage to federal, state, and local government employees, who are currently left out. It would strengthen whistleblower protections, including protection for workers who refuse dangerous work, and require employers to pay workers for time spent helping safety inspections. It would also raise fines dramatically for serious violations (from $70,000 to $700,000 for willful or repeated violations), allow criminal prosecution of corporate officers when safety violations kill or seriously injure workers, give injured workers and their families rights to follow safety investigations, and let the Labor Department enforce safety rules directly in states that run weak programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in dangerous jobs — construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, warehouses, and agriculture — plus the roughly 20 million state, county, and municipal government employees who currently have no federal safety-law protection. Families of workers killed on the job gain new rights to follow investigations and challenge lenient settlements. Workers who report injuries or refuse unsafe work gain stronger protection from retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in hazardous jobs and their families

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA's safety coverage to federal, state, and local government employees, closing a gap in the 1970 law that excluded them.
Raises maximum civil penalties for willful or repeated safety violations from $70,000 to $700,000, adjusts penalties annually for inflation, and allows daily fines for failing to fix serious hazards.

Allows criminal prosecution with prison terms up to 10 years for an employer whose knowing safety violation kills a worker, and defines 'employer' to include corporate officers and directors personally.

Strengthens whistleblower protections, including protecting employees who refuse work they reasonably believe will cause serious injury, and extends the time limit for filing retaliation complaints to 180 days.
Gives injured workers and family members of workers killed on the job the right to meet with investigators, receive citations, and be heard before settlements are negotiated.

Prohibits employers from discouraging injury reporting, requires prompt reporting of deaths, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye losses, and guarantees workers no loss of pay for participating in safety inspections.
Lets the Labor Department step in with its own enforcement when a state's workplace safety program fails to comply with its plan, and requires periodic outside review of state programs.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in hazardous industries, who would face fines up to $700,000 for willful or repeated violations, daily fines for unfixed hazards, possible criminal liability reaching individual executives, and stronger state-level enforcement. State governments would bear the cost of extending safety coverage to their own employees.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real costs on employers: penalties for willful or repeated violations rise tenfold, failure-to-correct fines rise tenfold, and any exposed employee can count as a separate violation. Small businesses with thin margins may find the compliance burden heavy.
Extending coverage to state and local government employees shifts enforcement and compliance costs onto state budgets, which is why states get 12 to 36 months to conform their plans.

Criminal penalties for workplace deaths raise questions about proportionality, since employer liability already exists through civil penalties and state law; the bill would put corporate officers at personal risk of prison.
The bill directs regulators to electronically report and publicly post injury data by employer, which employers argue could be misused to single out companies without full context.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to the population most exposed to workplace injury and death, and the costs fall on the employers whose practices create the hazards, which is the intended design of a safety law. The honest objections are the burden on small businesses from tenfold penalty increases and the cost to state budgets of covering public employees. The bill also contains genuine guardrails: stay procedures for employers contesting citations, a 'reasonable person' standard for refusing dangerous work, and protections against duplicative federal agency rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee in April 2025 and has had no further action since — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Courtney (D-CT) introduced the bill on April 28, 2025, with 41 Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day.
The complete action history shows no action after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote in committee, and no consideration on the House floor.
All 41 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, in a House where Republicans hold 223 seats to 217 for Democrats and 1 Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing higher safety penalties and individual executives facing potential criminal liability are better off with the bill stalled, since none of its fines, reporting requirements, or victim rights take effect. State governments also avoid the cost of extending safety coverage to their employees.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic: the sponsor and all 41 cosponsors are House Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored or acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, warehousing)
industries.note: These employers would face fines up to $700,000 for willful or repeated violations, daily fines for unfixed hazards, mandatory injury reporting, and potential criminal prosecution of officers for safety-related deaths. Their interest in avoiding these costs runs against workers' interest in safer job sites.

State and local government employers would become subject to federal safety standards for the first time, bearing compliance and enforcement costs. The same provision is the bill's main gain for the roughly 20 million public employees who currently have no federal safety-law coverage.

industries.industry: Workers' compensation and employer-side defense interests
industries.note: Victims' rights provisions give families a voice in settlements and before the safety review commission, and the bill bars arbitration clauses from waiving whistleblower rights, which would increase contestation of safety cases.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican majority in the House and no Republican cosponsors, a bill referred to the Education and Workforce Committee without a hearing or markup is unlikely to advance further this Congress. Its realistic paths are reintroduction in a future Congress or incorporation into a larger package if control of the chamber changes.
